extracted.intended_audience: general readers and social reformers interested in urban poverty and tenement conditions (late 19th-century New York)
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive social-reportage on gangs, working women, and pauperism in New York tenements, documenting causes, statistics, and human examples to persuade reformers and the public. Focuses on lived conditions, charitable classifications, and institutional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worthy of continuous relief
rubrics_metrics.description: 327 worthy of continuous relief, or 6.4 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described in the Charity Organization Society's classification of 5,169 investigated cases; these are the utterly helpless—orphans, cripples, or the very aged—who require ongoing support rather than temporary assistance or employment opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worthy of temporary relief
rubrics_metrics.description: 1,269 worthy of temporary relief, or 24.4 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those needing a short-term 'lift' to set them on the road to independence (or, if misapplied, toward permanent pauperism). The society treats these as cases where limited assistance may restore self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: In need of work rather than relief
rubrics_metrics.description: 2,698 in need of work, rather than relief, or 52.2 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority of investigated cases: able-bodied persons destitute because they have no work and are unable to find any. The recommended response is employment assistance rather than ongoing charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unworthy of relief
rubrics_metrics.description: 875 unworthy of relief, or 17 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those judged to be frauds or 'professional beggars'—training children to beg and otherwise exploiting charity. The text treats this as a distinct category to be excluded from relief and as a social problem to be addressed by policy and enforcement.
